title: Efficient Ternary Computation of Optimal Ate Pairing on BLS27 Curves
abstract: The computation of optimal Ate pairings on elliptic curves with embedding degree $k=27$ (BLS27) is highly relevant for achieving the 256-bit security level, especially in the context of recent advances in the Number Field Sieve (NFS) and its variants (exTNFS, SexTNFS). Traditional binary approaches fail to fully exploit the degree-3 extension tower of $\Fpk{27}$. In this work, we propose an efficient ternary version of the Miller loop, restricting the seed representation to sparse ternary digits $\{0, 1\}$ to streamline point operations and eliminate costly inversions. Furthermore, we generate two new parameter seeds tailored for exTNFS and SexTNFS security levels. These seeds feature sparse ternary representations that simultaneously guarantee the efficiency of the Miller loop and allow the full exploitation of cyclotomic cubing in $\mathbb{F}_{p^{27}}$ during the hard part of the final exponentiation. Compared to the state of the art binary approach by Fouotsa et al. (2020), our exTNFS seed yields a $22\%$ improvement in the overall optimal Ate pairing computation cost. Concurrently, our proposed SexTNFS seed ensures a higher level of security against the most advanced NFS variants.

                                               Abstract
      The computation of optimal Ate pairings on elliptic curves with embedding degree k = 27
      (BLS27) is highly relevant for achieving the 256-bit security level, especially in the context
      of recent advances in the Number Field Sieve (NFS) and its variants (exTNFS, SexTNFS).
      Traditional binary approaches fail to fully exploit the degree-3 extension tower of Fp27 . In
      this work, we propose an efficient ternary version of the Miller loop, restricting the seed
      representation to sparse ternary digits {0, 1} to streamline point operations and eliminate
      costly inversions. Furthermore, we generate two new parameter seeds tailored for exTNFS
      and SexTNFS security levels. These seeds feature sparse ternary representations that si-
      multaneously guarantee the efficiency of the Miller loop and allow the full exploitation of
      cyclotomic cubing in Fp27 during the hard part of the final exponentiation. Compared to
      the state of the art binary approach by Fouotsa et al. (2020), our exTNFS seed yields a
      22% improvement in the overall optimal Ate pairing computation cost. Concurrently, our
      proposed SexTNFS seed ensures a higher level of security against the most advanced NFS
      variants.

Keywords: Optimal Ate pairing, BLS27 curves, Ternary Miller algorithm, Cyclotomic cubing,
Final exponentiation, exTNFS, SexTNFS.


1    Introduction
Pairing-based cryptography has enabled the realization of numerous advanced cryptographic
protocols, such as Identity-Based Encryption (IBE) [4], short signatures [5], and attribute-based
encryption [11]. The efficiency of these protocols relies heavily on the fast computation of bilinear
pairings, particularly the optimal Ate pairing, on pairing-friendly elliptic curves.
For a long time, curves with even embedding degrees (e.g., BN12, BLS12) were favored due
to the availability of quadratic twists and efficient binary Miller algorithms. However, recent
breakthroughs in the resolution of the Discrete Logarithm Problem (DLP) in finite fields using
the Number Field Sieve (NFS) and its variants, such as the Extended Tower NFS (exTNFS) and
Special exTNFS (SexTNFS), have necessitated a re-evaluation of parameter sizes. According to
Barbulescu and Duquesne [2], at the 256-bit security level, the extension field Fpk must be as
large as 218480 for exTNFS and 227410 for SexTNFS. For k = 27, this implies base field primes
p of roughly 684 and 1015 bits, respectively. BLS27 curves, with an embedding degree k = 27,
offer a practical resistance against these NFS variants. Indeed, the larger embedding degree
allows the extension field Fpk to reach the massive sizes required for 256-bit security without
requiring an impractically large base field prime p. Because 27 = 33 , the extension field Fp27
is naturally constructed as a tower of degree-3 extensions. In this tower, computing the cubing
in the cyclotomic subgroup of Fp27 is exceptionally cheap, allowing us to replace the traditional
square-and-multiply routine. Furthermore, the curve’s j-invariant of 0 allows for a cubic twist,

                                                    1
meaning the point operations for the first argument of the optimal Ate pairing can be performed
entirely in the smaller subfield.
Several works have investigated pairings on curves with odd embedding degrees and cubic twists.
Zhang and Lin [17] provided an early analysis of optimum pairing products at high security lev-
els, including k = 27. Fouotsa, El Mrabet, and Pecha [9] provided a detailed arithmetic and
cost estimation of operations in the tower extensions for k = 9, 15, 27, improving the theoret-
ical cost of the Miller loop and final exponentiation by applying the lattice-based method of
Fuentes-Castañeda et al. [10]. However, their approach relied on the traditional binary Miller
algorithm and binary exponentiation in the final exponentiation. More recently, Hayashida et
al. [12] proposed a new framework for efficient final exponentiation via cyclotomic structure,
directly factorizing the hard part using homogeneous cyclotomic polynomials. For odd embed-
ding degrees divisible by 3, where cyclotomic squaring is not available, Nanjo et al. [14] derived
an explicit formula for cyclotomic cubing. Ben Abdelghani and Haddaji [3] further optimized
these arithmetic operations, providing precise costs for Frobenius maps and demonstrating the
applicability of cyclotomic cubing to reduce final exponentiation costs for BLS27 by generat-
ing specific seeds. In this work, we build upon these advancements to present a fully ternary
framework for the entire optimal Ate pairing computation. Despite the structural advantages of
BLS27, the use of a binary Miller loop fails to fully exploit the base-3 structure of the extension
tower. In this paper, we adapt the entire pairing computation to exploit this base-3 representa-
tion. Our contributions are as follows. We provide the mathematical proofs about the ternary
version of Miller loop.
  1. Efficient ternary Miller loop: we introduce a ternary Miller algorithm that operates
     strictly on seeds with ternary digits in {0, 1}. This removes the need for the digit 2, avoiding
     precomputation of doublings and extra field multiplications, while exploiting cheap cubing
     in Fp27 .

  2. Optimal seeds for NFS Security: we generate and utilize specific seeds:

                                         x1 = 323 + 35 + 33 + 1

     for exTNFS (256-bit) and

                                 x2 = 332 + 331 + 327 + 322 + 310 + 1

     for SexTNFS (256-bit), both fitting our {0, 1} constraint.

  3. Cyclotomic Cubing in Final Exponentiation: we adapt the hard part of the final
     exponentiation to use ternary exponentiation via cyclotomic cubing.

  4. Complexity analysis and comparison: we give a detailed complexity analysis for the
     ternary Miller loop and provide a detailed cost estimation and compare our theoretical costs
     with the recent work by Fouotsa et al. [9]. Notably, we mathematically verify the exact
     congruence of p modulo 27 for both our seeds and theirs, correcting previous Frobenius
     cost assumptions and demonstrating substantial efficiency gains.
The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 recalls the fundamental definitions
of the BLS27 family, the optimal Ate pairing, and the arithmetic properties of the underlying
finite field extensions. Section 3 presents our novel ternary Miller algorithm, providing rigorous
mathematical proofs for its correctness, alongside our ternary exponentiation approach for the
hard part of the final exponentiation. Section 4 details the generation of our specific ternary
seeds and provides a comprehensive complexity analysis of both the Miller loop and the final
exponentiation. Section 5 contrasts our theoretical costs against the state of the art binary
approach by Fouotsa et al., highlighting the significant efficiency gains and security advantages
achieved by our method. Finally, Section 6 concludes the paper.

2.1   BLS27 Curves
The Barreto-Lynn-Scott (BLS) family with embedding degree k = 27, denoted BLS27, is pa-
rameterized by an integer x as [1]:

For a suitable integer x such that both p(x) and r(x) are prime, the elliptic curve E is defined

The hard part, raising the result to the power d, is the computational bottleneck. Fouotsa et
al. [9] computed this using the lattice-based method of Fuentes-Castañeda et al. [10], expressing
d as a polynomial in x and evaluating it via a vectorial addition chain.

using homogeneous cyclotomic polynomials. For the BLS27 family, where r(x) = (x18 +x9 +1)/3,

3     Pairing using ternary computation
In this section, we present a ternary version of Miller algorithm and detail the mathematical
proofs that ensure its correctness, alongside our ternary exponentiation approach for the final
exponentiation.

3.1   The Ternary Miller Algorithm
We propose a ternary version of Miller’s algorithm that evaluates fx,Q (P ) by processing the
base-3 representation of x. To maximize efficiency, we restrict the ternary digits to di ∈ {0, 1},
avoiding the digit 2. This eliminates the need to precompute 2Q and evaluate the corresponding
line function. The Miller ternary loop is given in Algorithm 2.
As established for the binary algorithm, we use Q′ and T to denote the points as they are
represented on the twist E ′ (Fp9 ). The rational line functions are evaluated at P ∈ E(Fp ) using


                                                 6
the images of these points under the twist isomorphism ψ. This allows the point operations
(triplings and additions) to be performed efficiently over the subfield Fp9 , while the function
updates (cubings and multiplications) are performed in Fp27 . Evaluating the lines at P ∈ E(Fp )
allows for denominator elimination techniques, where multiplying by the appropriate conjugate
factor pushes the denominators into a proper subfield of Fp27 , which is then eliminated during
the final exponentiation.

3.2   Ternary Hard Part of Final Exponentiation
The most computationally expensive operation in the hard part of the final exponentiation is the
exponentiation by the seed x within the cyclotomic subgroup. Previous works, such as Fouotsa
et al. [9], evaluated this exponentiation using the binary representation of x, performing a
cyclotomic squaring at each step, followed by a cyclotomic multiplication depending on whether
the current bit was 1. However, in the extension field Fp27 , fast cyclotomic squaring is not
available (only classical squaring is supported), as the embedding degree k = 27 does not allow
the standard squaring-friendly cyclotomic structure. Fortunately, as demonstrated by Nanjo et
al. [14] and Ben Abdelghani et al. [3], an efficient cyclotomic cubing formula is supported in this
context. To fully exploit the efficiency of this operation, we specifically searched for seeds that
are sparse in their ternary representation. This ternary sparsity is a critical design choice, as it
simultaneously guarantees the efficiency of both the Miller loop and the final exponentiation. We
successfully generated two sparse ternary seeds that achieve the 256-bit security level against
exTNFS and SexTNFS attacks [2]. We generate two ternary seeds satisfying the following
criteria:

    • Both parameters p(x) and r(x) must be prime.

    • The seed must guarantee a 256-bit security level against NFS variants.

    • The ternary representation of the seed must be highly sparse to minimize the number of
      addition steps in the Miller loop.

    • The ternary digits must be restricted to {0, 1} to avoid the precomputation of 2Q and
      eliminate extra cyclotomic inversions.

With respect to the above conditions, we were able to generated seeds are as follows:

    • exTNFS Seed: x1 = 323 + 35 + 33 + 1. This seed has a ternary loop length of l1 = 23 and
      a Hamming weight of hw = 4.

    • SexTNFS Seed: x2 = 332 + 331 + 327 + 322 + 310 + 1. This seed has a ternary loop length
      of l2 = 33 and a Hamming weight of hw = 6.

To accommodate varying application requirements, we generated two distinct seeds targeting
exTNFS and SexTNFS resistance, respectively. Both seeds maintain the 256-bit security level
but offer a deliberate trade-off between performance and maximum cryptographic strength. The
exTNFS seed is optimized for scenarios where computational efficiency is the primary objective.
Conversely, for applications requiring the highest level of security against the more powerful
SexTNFS attacks, the SexTNFS seed should be selected, acknowledging a marginal reduction
in computational speed. Because of the presence of the cyclotomic cubing, we express the final
exponentiation complexity as follows:

                      I27 + 8 × M27 + Ccyc27 + F27 + 2 × Ex−1 + 17 × Ex .                       (3)

6    Conclusion
In this paper, we presented an efficient ternary framework for computing the optimal Ate pairing
on BLS27 curves. By restricting the seed x to sparse ternary digits {0, 1}, we developed a
faster Miller algorithm that uses cheap cubing in the Fp27 extension tower, and we rigorously
proved its correctness. For the final exponentiation, we replaced standard binary methods with
ternary exponentiation, using cyclotomic cubing and a new chaining trick to greatly reduce the
computational cost.
Our two proposed seeds offer a clear trade-off between speed and security. The exTNFS seed
makes the pairing computation 22% faster than the binary approach by Fouotsa et al., while
ensuring that both p and r are prime—which the previous baseline seed failed to do. The
SexTNFS seed is slower due to its larger size, but it provides the highest security against ad-
vanced SexTNFS attacks and also guarantees valid primes. Together, they show that our ternary
method is both faster and more secure for BLS27 curves.
For future work, the pairing could be sped up further by improving basic arithmetic in Fp27 , such
as finding faster formulas for standard cubing and squaring. Additionally, finding new algebraic
shortcuts to reduce the cost of the point tripling step in the Miller loop remains a promising
direction.
